# Query Plans, Reporting Indexes, and the Performance Baseline

**Work item:** Phase 5 / increment 5.7
**Rules:** NFR-02 (the dashboard answers within three seconds), BR-U01–BR-U06, BR-P05
**Artefact:** [`artifacts/phase-5/reporting-baseline.md`](../../artifacts/phase-5/reporting-baseline.md) — regenerated by `scripts/run-reporting-performance-baseline.ps1`

## The plans are captured, not transcribed

The reporting layer issues a mixture of Entity Framework translations and raw aggregates. Running
`EXPLAIN` over SQL copied into a test file would produce evidence about the copy: it would drift
the moment the reader changed, and nothing would fail. The harness instead switches on
`auto_explain` with `log_analyze`, `log_buffers` and `log_nested_statements`, runs a scenario, and
slices the server log around it. Every plan recorded is the plan PostgreSQL chose for the statement
the application actually sent, and a query that is added or reshaped later shows up in the evidence
without anyone remembering to add it.

Plan capture and timing are separate passes, because `log_analyze` instruments every plan node and
inflates the very durations NFR-02 is stated in.

## The fixture

A scenario is a whole screen's worth of reads, not one query — `HomeController.Index` issues eight,
and a dashboard with seven fast queries and one slow one is a slow dashboard.

| | |
|---|---|
| Clients / websites / environments | 6 / 24 / 48 |
| Endpoints / monitors | 96 / 192 |
| History | 90 days, both default cadences (5 min production, 15 min elsewhere) |
| Check results | ~1.67 million |
| Unfiltered 30-day window | ~556,000 samples aggregated |

That is well above what this project's own deployment would carry, which is the point: the headroom
is measured rather than assumed. The registry is built through the real services so the rows carry
real fingerprints, snapshots and monitor defaults; only the history is written set-based, because
1.67 million samples through the change tracker would measure Entity Framework rather than
PostgreSQL.

Two of the tables involved carry `DEFERRABLE` per-row constraint triggers, which queue one event per
inserted row and settle them at commit — correct for an application that inserts a handful of rows
per check, impractical for a bulk load. The load therefore runs under `session_replication_role =
replica`, and every invariant those triggers and the foreign keys enforce is then re-checked as a
set operation with the role back to normal. Skipping the checks without re-running them would mean
measuring queries over data that might not be valid.

Both an administrator and a viewer scoped to one client are measured. `ApplyEndpointScope`
short-circuits for global access, so an administrator never exercises the visibility scope at all;
measuring only the administrator would leave the grant subqueries every other role pays for on the
critical path entirely unmeasured.

## What the first capture showed

Every hot reporting query had the same plan: **two parallel sequential scans and a hash join**,
spilling to temporary files.

```
Aggregate  (actual time=889.199..925.507 rows=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=11803 read=58930, temp read=14716 written=14308
  ->  Parallel Hash Join  (rows=185280)
        Hash Cond: (check_row.id = result.logical_check_id)
        ->  Parallel Seq Scan on logical_check   (rows=555840)
              Filter: (endpoint_monitor_id = ANY (...))
        ->  Parallel Seq Scan on check_result    (rows=185280)
              Filter: (measured_at >= ... AND measured_at < ...)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 370560
```

The cause is structural rather than a missing index. Every reporting aggregate selects **one set of
monitors over one window**, but the monitor lived on `logical_check` and the measurement instant
lived on `check_result`. No index can serve a predicate pair split across two tables, so each
aggregate degenerated into a full scan of both and a hash join between them. Narrowing to one client
barely helped: `logical_check` was still scanned end to end.

## The change the evidence asked for

`check_result` now carries `endpoint_monitor_id`, with a covering index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ix_check_result_monitor_measured_at
    ON web_health.check_result (endpoint_monitor_id, measured_at)
    INCLUDE (outcome, counts_for_uptime, total_duration_ms, monitor_source);
```

Both halves of the predicate are now on one table, and the columns every aggregate reads are carried
in the index.

What the captured plans actually show is worth stating precisely, because it is less than the index
design allows. Filtered scenarios use the new index and drop from two sequential scans and a hash
join to a **bitmap index scan plus a bitmap heap scan** — a large improvement, but not an index-only
scan. `INCLUDE` columns make an index-only scan *possible*; PostgreSQL only takes it when the
visibility map says the pages are all-visible, which a freshly bulk-loaded, never-vacuumed table does
not satisfy. The evidence here therefore demonstrates a much narrower scan, not heap-free execution,
and no claim of heap-free execution should be made from it.

The unfiltered whole-fleet case is different again: with every monitor selected the monitor predicate
is not selective, so the planner reasonably prefers scanning by time or sequentially. The index helps
where there is a filter to exploit, and the measured improvement is concentrated there.

**The denormalised value cannot drift.** The foreign key is composite —
`(logical_check_id, endpoint_monitor_id)` referencing `logical_check (id, endpoint_monitor_id)` —
so the database refuses any sample whose monitor is not the monitor of the check it belongs to. This
is not a new idea in this schema: `certificate_observation`, `endpoint_health`, `execution_lease` and
`incident_evidence` already use exactly this guard, which is why the required unique constraint on
`logical_check (id, endpoint_monitor_id)` was already there.

The migration adds the column nullable, backfills it from the check each sample already belongs to,
and only then tightens it to `NOT NULL` and adds the key. Adding it `NOT NULL` with a placeholder
default would write a monitor identity that is not any monitor, and the composite foreign key would
then refuse every existing row.

### This migration needs a maintenance window

It is not an online migration and is not written as one. In a single transaction it rewrites every
row of `check_result` twice (the backfill, then the `NOT NULL` rewrite), builds two indexes, and
validates a composite foreign key across the whole table. On a database already carrying real
history that means an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock held for the duration: check finalization would block,
and rolling back late is as expensive as going forward.

That is an acceptable trade here and is stated rather than hidden. This is a single-operator personal
project with no availability commitment, the schema is applied explicitly by an operator running
`dotnet ef database update` (never implicitly at startup), and the alternative — expand, batched
backfill, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, contract — is
several migrations and a multi-deploy sequence whose only benefit is availability this project does
not require. If a real deployment with an availability requirement is ever pursued, this migration is
the worked example of what that sequence would have to replace.

**Apply it with monitoring paused, and take a backup first.**

Four queries lost their join outright: the summary aggregate, the per-monitor aggregate behind the
current-health table, the daily trend, and the diagnostics card's last-completed-check read.

## The comparability warning was both the dominant cost and wrong

BR-P05's dataset-level warning was the largest single statement on every scenario measured — 48% of
the default dashboard's database time, 41% of the ninety-day view, and 65–74% of the filtered ones.
Investigating the cost is what exposed the defect.

It asked whether more than one `configuration_fingerprint` appeared across the window. A fingerprint
hashes the endpoint's **normalized URL** among other inputs, so two different monitors always carry
different fingerprints. Comparing them across a fleet therefore answers "are these different
monitors?" — always yes. Measured against the fixture:

| | |
|---|---|
| Distinct fingerprints fleet-wide | 96 (one per endpoint) |
| Monitors whose configuration actually changed in the window | **0** |

So the dashboard reported *"the check configuration changed across these results"* on every report
covering more than one endpoint, while nothing had changed. A warning that is permanently on carries
no information, and worse, it trains a reader to ignore the one case where it matters.

"The configuration changed" is a question about **one monitor over time**. The query now groups by
monitor and asks whether that monitor's own samples span more than one fingerprint, with the sources
collected in the same pass. `PerformanceComparability` documents the contract explicitly so the
distinction cannot be lost again.

Correcting it was close to free: 861 ms against 908 ms for the wrong answer, on a warm 30-day window.
The cost is the join to `check_configuration_snapshot`, not the aggregation — sources alone, read
from the covering index with no join, still cost 565 ms because half a million samples must be read
either way. Removing that join would mean carrying configuration identity on the sample, a second
denormalisation; the measurements below show it would not by itself close the remaining gap, so it is
recorded rather than done.

## A correctness defect the baseline surfaced

Running the reporting layer against a real cluster for the first time failed immediately, and not on
performance:

```
The LINQ expression '... .OrderBy(ti => new MonitorRow(
    DbSet<EndpointHealth>() ... DbSet<Incident>() ...).ClientName)'
could not be translated.
```

`SelectMonitors` ordered and filtered the **projection** rather than the entities. For an
administrator that happened to translate; for every other role the visibility scope contributed its
own grant subqueries and the provider gave up. The dashboard, the CSV export, the certificate card,
the diagnostics card and the incident list would all have failed for any viewer or developer.

The fix moves the ordering and both filters to the monitor's own columns, before anything is
projected:

- **Ordering** is applied to entity columns, which also lets PostgreSQL sort on real columns.
- **Health status** is filtered through the one-to-one `EndpointHealth` navigation. `Unknown` is the
  absence of a confirmation, so it is the one status that also matches a monitor with no health row.
- **Monitor type** for the certificate card goes through `SelectMonitors` as one more filter applied
  where every other filter is applied, rather than narrowing the projected rows afterwards.

The projection also reads health through that navigation now — one left join instead of two
correlated subqueries per row.

The 5.5 gate would have caught this; it had simply never been run against a database. It now sweeps
every status and monitor-type combination for a scoped reader across all five surfaces, so a
selection that only composes for an administrator cannot pass as working. Two stale entries in the
foundation gate's expected-migration list were also corrected, which would have failed that gate on
its first run.

## How the measurement is taken

One decision matters enough to record. The harness scripts connect with pooling disabled so a
database can be dropped and recreated between steps, but the measured services force pooling back
on. Timing through an unpooled string charges a fresh TCP connection and authentication handshake to
every statement a screen issues — about two and a half seconds per dashboard on this fixture, none of
which the application pays. That artefact initially made the reporting work look roughly twice as
expensive as it is, and very nearly drove the wrong conclusion.

Enabling pooling then broke plan capture, which is worth recording as the same class of mistake in
the other direction: `session_preload_libraries` is read when a session starts, and `pg_reload_conf`
does not reach sessions that already exist, so the pool handed back connections opened before
`auto_explain` was switched on and nothing was logged. The harness clears the pool after the reload.

Full per-statement plans are in
[`artifacts/phase-5/reporting-baseline.md`](../../artifacts/phase-5/reporting-baseline.md),
regenerated on every run.

## Measured result against NFR-02

Fixture: 96 endpoints, 192 monitors, 90 days, 1,667,520 samples — deliberately above what this
project's own deployment carries. Ten iterations per scenario; the reported P95 is the slowest of the
ten, so it reads high rather than low.

| Scenario | P95 | NFR-02 |
|---|---:|---|
| Dashboard — unfiltered, 30 days *(the default view)* | 2,673 ms | within budget |
| Dashboard — one client, 30 days | 701 ms | within budget |
| Dashboard — viewer scoped to one client, 30 days | 735 ms | within budget |
| Dashboard — unfiltered, 90 days | 7,585 ms | **over budget** |
| CSV export — unfiltered, 30 days | 674 ms | not a dashboard |

The default dashboard and every filtered view meet the three-second budget, the filtered ones with
roughly four times' headroom. One case does not: the whole fleet over a ninety-day window.

## Daily aggregates: the decision this evidence forces

Where the ninety-day view's 6,213 ms of database work goes: comparability 2,527 ms, trend 1,835 ms,
summary 1,468 ms, per-monitor 368 ms. Those are four aggregates over the same ~1.6 million samples,
grouped four different ways.

This is the arithmetic that settles it. Even removing the comparability query **entirely** leaves
about 3.7 seconds of database work and roughly five seconds of wall clock — still over budget. No
index closes this gap, because the aggregate genuinely has to read every sample in the window; an
index can only decide how fast it finds them. Query-level work is therefore finished: what remains is
a data-volume problem, and pre-reducing the window is the only thing that addresses it.

That makes the aggregate question a scope decision rather than an optimisation one, and it is
recorded here unresolved rather than settled quietly:

- **Bound what the dashboard offers.** The dashboard defaults to thirty days and meets the budget
  there; the widest windows are already served well by the CSV export at 674 ms. Declaring the
  dashboard's supported window and leaving long-period analysis to the export closes NFR-02 as
  specified, with no new schema.
- **Build daily aggregates now.** Closes every window, and is a whole increment: schema, incremental
  maintenance, backfill, and tests proving the rollup agrees with the raw samples it replaces.

Phase 7 remains the natural home for the second option, because a daily rollup and a retention policy
are one decision — retention determines how far back raw samples exist, which determines what a
rollup must cover and when it becomes the only surviving record of a day. Building the rollup first
would mean designing it against a retention policy that does not exist yet.

`ReportingPerformanceBaselineTests` asserts the budget for every dashboard scenario, so it fails
today on the ninety-day case. That failure is the record of the open decision and should not be
silenced by narrowing what is asserted; it is resolved by taking one of the two options above.

## Verification evidence

- `ReportingPerformanceBaselineTests` — seeds the fixture, verifies the seeded history satisfies
  every invariant the bulk load bypassed, captures a plan per scenario, and asserts the dashboard
  scenarios against NFR-02.
- `scripts/run-reporting-performance-baseline.ps1` — disposable PostgreSQL 18 cluster, explicit
  `dotnet ef database update` (never an implicit migration at startup), then the harness.
- The migration applies cleanly to an empty database, which is the path every baseline run exercises
  (migrate, then seed). Its behaviour against a database **already carrying history** — the path the
  backfill exists for — is not yet covered by an automated check; that gap is real and is the next
  thing to close, by seeding first and migrating second.
- The baseline is deliberately **not** part of the delivery gate. It writes millions of rows and runs
  every scenario twenty times; folding that into the correctness gate would make the gate too slow to
  run often, and a slow gate stops being run. It is skipped unless its environment variables are set.
